metadata.title: Products, Squares, and Quadratic Age Relations
metadata.description: Use products and simple quadratic equations to determine ages, then reject values that cannot represent valid ages.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the age model from a clearly labeled timeline, derive each equation before calculating, work through intermediate steps, and check the answer against the original age relation. Targeted remedial branches explain the likely misconception and lead to a fresh, related retry.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 8 “Problems on Ages,” printed pages 264–277. Approved scope: Handle chapter-level age problems involving the product of two ages together with their sum, difference, or another linear relation. Build the equation from the stated relationship, use factor pairs or simple factoring to find candidate ages, and explain why two algebraic roots may appear while only one pair may satisfy the people’s age order and the problem's time conditions. Where a sum and product are known, connect them to a quadratic only at an elementary factoring level. Check candidates in the original product and linear condition; reject negative, fractional, or otherwise inadmissible values only when the stated context or integer-age assumption requires it. Do not teach general quadratic formula methods beyond the source level.

content.text: Let’s build age equations by keeping every person and every date explicit. Work through the timeline lesson before using the practice questions to check your reasoning.
A product alone does not determine two ages: many pairs multiply to the same number. Combine the product with a sum, difference, or ratio to restrict the possibilities.
If two ages have sum S and product P, call one age x and the other S−x. Then x(S−x)=P. At this level, factor pairs are often the clearest route: find two numbers whose sum is S and product is P.

For ages with a known difference d and product P, write the younger age as x and older as x+d. Then x(x+d)=P. Test factor pairs or factor the resulting quadratic, retaining only ages that fit the stated ordering.

A quadratic can produce two algebraic roots because either age may appear as x in a symmetric equation. The story determines which root is the younger age and whether a negative or non-real candidate is admissible.
Use the identity (x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2 only when it simplifies the supplied information. Rearranging gives x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2−2xy. Substitute the known sum and product carefully, preserving the factor 2.
A square relation is also constrained by age meaning. If a problem states a positive age, reject negative roots. Do not reject fractional ages unless the problem requires completed integer ages.

Check both original conditions after factoring. A candidate can satisfy a manipulated equation if a sign was lost or if the wrong factor pair was selected; multiply and add the proposed ages directly.
For a real-world result, report ages in the requested order and units. A product of ages has units of years squared, while the final individual ages are in years.
